title: Sepharad
hookLine: Jewish life in Spain under Muslim and then Christian rule

cards: Near the end of the little book of Obadiah, one of the Prophets, there's a line about exiles from Jerusalem living in a faraway place called Sepharad. The verse never says where that is. One verse, no map.

Much later, Jews on the Iberian peninsula, in what is now Spain and Portugal, read that verse and heard their own address in it. Sepharad became the Hebrew name for Spain, and the Jews of Spain became Sephardim.
Yesterday a family tree gave a name to the north. Today a prophet's line gives a name to the west.

teach.h: THE CAPTIVITY OF JERUSALEM, THAT IS IN SEPHARAD.
teach.b: Here is the line, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "the captivity of Jerusalem, that is in Sepharad." Some readers point to a city in Asia Minor.
But Jewish tradition, through the Aramaic translation and the medieval commentators, heard Spain, and that reading stuck.

A people far from Jerusalem found themselves named in the Bible, as exiles who still belonged to Jerusalem. Some readers hear a double feeling in that, at home and not at home, and it returns in the Sephardi story.
That story has two long chapters.
In the first, much of Spain was ruled by Muslim dynasties, with a capital at Córdoba.
Jews spoke Arabic, read Arabic philosophy and poetry, served as doctors, translators and officials, and wrote Hebrew poetry that borrowed Arabic meters.

Over the next days you'll meet some of them: a courtier, a poet who led an army, a philosopher of the heart. It wasn't paradise. There were persecutions under some rulers, and Jews lived as a protected but lower class.
But it was a long season of learning. In the second chapter, Christian kingdoms took the peninsula back, step by step.
Jews lived under Christian kings, again as advisers, tax collectors and doctors, and again with protection that could turn into danger. That chapter ends hard, and we'll get there.
Through both chapters, Sephardi Jews built their own customs, prayer melodies, and a language families carried far beyond Spain: Ladino, or Judeo-Spanish.

teach.h: A PLACE, A MEMORY, A WAY OF PRAYING.
teach.b: Sepharad is a place, then a memory, then a way of praying.

how: Sephardi Jews keep their own prayer rite, melodies and customs, and some families still speak or sing in Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish their ancestors carried after leaving Spain.

games.q: you are a Jew in medieval Spain reading Obadiah. the verse mentions exiles from Jerusalem in a place called Sepharad. how does your tradition read it?
o: as a place no one can know, so it is ignored.
as Spain, the land you live in.
games.why: Jewish tradition heard Spain in Obadiah's Sepharad, and the name stuck: the Jews of Spain became Sephardim, exiles who still belonged to Jerusalem.

practice: Choose one word from a language your family, or a friend's family, once spoke, Spanish, Ladino, Arabic, Yiddish, and say it quietly. Who taught it to you, and how far did it travel to reach you?
If you don't have one, take a Spanish word like casa, house, and think of all the houses it has named; if you pray, keep the word in mind as you do.

wordCard.voice: Sepharad. A place named once in Obadiah that Jewish tradition read as Spain, and so the name of the Jews of Spain and their descendants. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a place named in Obadiah 1:20, read by Jewish tradition as Spain.
